podcast.title: Signature Telecaster Model (2021)
podcast.body: In 2021, Chrissie Hynde became one of the few female guitarists to receive her own signature model, an ice-blue Telecaster. This guitar was based on a 1965 version she purchased in New York City in 1981, and its characteristic chiming chords are integral to her sound. "In 2021, she became one of the few female guitarists to have her own signature model, an ice-blue Telecaster, based on a 1965 version she bought in New York City in 1981."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Advocate for Simple Minds
podcast.body: Chrissie Hynde, lead singer of The Pretenders, played a crucial role in convincing Simple Minds to record "Don't You (Forget About Me)" for *The Breakfast Club* soundtrack. As the wife of Simple Minds' singer Jim Kerr at the time, she asked everyone in the band to reconsider their initial reluctance, which ultimately led them to record their biggest hit. "But the label kept up the pressure and Chrissy Holland at the pretenders, who was married to Singer Jim Carr at the time, asked everyone in the band to reconsider."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Attempted Marriage to Sid Vicious for Work Permit
podcast.body: While working illegally in the UK, Chrissie Hynde, then employed at Malcolm McLaren's "Sex" shop, paid Sid Vicious two pounds to marry her so she could obtain a work permit. The plan was thwarted when the office where they intended to marry was closed on the chosen day. "She paid Sid two pounds to marry her so she could get a work permit. And it almost happened too, but the day they went to get married, the office was closed."

podcast.title: Early Punk Scene Figure and Guitar Teacher
podcast.body: Chrissie Hynde was an American living in London at the heart of the burgeoning punk rock scene. She was a more skilled guitarist than many of her peers, even providing lessons to novices like Steve Jones and Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols. Her rhythm guitar style was heavily influenced by James Brown's band. "She gave lessons to novices like Steve Jones and Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding The Pretenders – Lead Woman in Rock
podcast.body: After several attempts to form a band, including discussions with Mick Jones before he formed The Clash, Chrissie Hynde founded The Pretenders in 1978. She was unique in late 1970s rock as a woman who not only sang lead and fronted the band but also played rhythm guitar and wrote most of their music, thriving in the receptive British punk environment. "Chrissy formed the pretenders in 1978. Here we have a woman singing lead, acting as front person and spokesperson and playing with in guitar. Not exactly a common thing in rock in the late 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact of "Ohio"
podcast.body: Chrissie Hynde expressed her relief and gratitude upon the release of Neil Young's "Ohio," feeling that Young was providing a voice for the Kent State students who were still in shock and finishing their semester from home. This sentiment highlights the song's immediate emotional and social impact on young people. "Chrissy Hine, who would go on, of course, to have her own band, the pretenders, said that when that song came out, she was glad She was glad that Neil Young was offering to be the voice for the students who were still in shock and finishing out the semester from home and mailing in their assignments"

podcast.title: Punk Pioneer
podcast.body: Chrissie Hynde of The Pretenders was a pioneer who took advantage of punk rock values, inspiring many to express themselves regardless of background or gender. "Suzy Su, of Suzy in the Banshee's, members of the Slitz, Pauli Styrene of X-Ray Specks, Chrissy Hinder, the Pretenders, Patty Smith, and so many more. They were all pioneers and they all inspired many people, women, but also men, to do what they did."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Songwriting Philosophy
podcast.body: Hynde's approach to songwriting focused on the intriguing idea of crafting the best melodies over the fewest possible chord changes, emphasizing melodic strength and simplicity. "And when it came to songwriting, she became intrigued at how some of the best melodies could be written over the top of the fewest number of chord changes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Taylor Hawkins and the Co-Tale Riders (2006)
xref.body: In 2006, Taylor Hawkins formed his own band, Taylor Hawkins and the Co-Tale Riders, a name reflecting his sense of humor and humbleness. The band featured crack session musicians and released three albums, collaborating with figures like Roger Taylor and Brian May (Queen), Nancy Wilson (Heart), Joe Walsh (Eagles), Chrissie Hynde (Pretenders), and LeAnn Rimes. "The first came in 2006 when he formed a band called Taylor Hawkins and the Co-Tale Riders."

xref.title: Blackie O'Nassis Death (June 13, 2023) – Drummer on Pulp Fiction's "Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon"; Age 57, Cause Unknown
xref.body: John Rowan, who played under the name Blackie O'Nassis, was the drummer for Urge Overkill — the Chicago band whose cover of Neil Diamond's "Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon" (1967) appears in the famous dance scene in *Pulp Fiction*. The band was also a cult favorite in the alt-rock community and opened for Nirvana on the *Nevermind* tour, during which they befriended Kurt Cobain, Chrissie Hynde of the Pretenders, and Liz Phair. Blackie left the band in 1996; there were reports of heroin use and at least one arrest. The cause of his death on June 13, 2023, at age 57 was never disclosed. "As for the cause of his death on June 13th, 2023, we have no idea."

xref.title: Chrissie Hynde Association
xref.body: Chrissie Hynde of The Pretenders worked in Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop during the Sex Pistols' formative years. She also famously considered marrying Sid Vicious, the band's bassist, primarily to secure the British equivalent of a green card and remain in the UK. "Along with working in Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop in the earliest days of the Sex Pistols, she also wrote about punk in one of the British music magazines."

xref.body: Chrissie Hynde, frontwoman of The Pretenders, was one of the artists who collaborated with Taylor Hawkins on his Co-Tale Riders albums. Her involvement underscores the diverse range of musicians Hawkins brought into his side project. "Chrissy Hinder, the Pretenders."

xref.title: Chrissie Hynde's Punk Credentials
xref.body: Lead singer Chrissie Hynde, originally from Akron, Ohio, moved to the UK and became deeply involved in the early punk scene, working at Malcolm McLaren's shop "Sex" and playing guitar in bands that morphed into The Clash and The Damned, even considering a marriage of convenience with Sid Vicious. "So yeah, a lot of bonafide punk credentials."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Continued Activity
xref.body: Despite being nearly 70 years old, Chrissie Hynde remains active in music. "even though she's nearly 70, she is still going."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Influences
xref.body: From childhood, Chrissie Hynde loved the guitar and, due to a scarcity of female role models, drew inspiration from James Brown's guitarist. She also admired artists like Alice Cooper, The Stooges, and Jeff Beck. "She loved the guitar from the time she was a kid. With few female role models, she looked to the guitarist employed by James Brown. She loved Alice Cooper and the stooages and Jeff Beck."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Evolution from Chrissie Hynde's Band
xref.body: One of the short-lived British punk bands in which Chrissie Hynde played guitar during her early days in London later evolved into The Clash, establishing a direct link between her punk roots and the formation of this major punk act. "She also played guitar in several short-lived British punk bands, one of which later revolved into the clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Evolution from London SS
xref.body: The Clash evolved out of a prominent British punk band known as the London SS, which was famous for never playing a gig. Many musicians passed through London SS, including Chrissie Hynde, who later formed The Pretenders. "The Clash evolved out of the most famous British punk band to never play a gig. They were called the London SS."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Exotic Pornography Collection
xref.body: Brian Eno is known to have a large and extensive collection of exotic pornography, a fact he openly discussed. An article in the "NME" in 1974 by Chrissie Hynde provided proof, where Eno described pornography as a "highly developed art form" and detailed his collection, particularly "pornographic playing cards," some of which featured on his "Used-Stood Observer" record covers. He likened the directness of pornographic photography to rock music. "I have such beautiful pornography. I'll show you my collection sometime."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Fighting Sexism and Becoming a Role Model
xref.body: Despite the "tremendous bias against female players" and "awful" sexism prevalent in the 1970s, Chrissie Hynde persevered, using the "Free For All" attitude of punk to prove her guitar-playing abilities were on par with men, eventually becoming a role model herself. "The sexism was awful. But Chrissy fought through it and in the process became a role model herself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation and Search for a Singer
xref.body: Garbage was formed by producers Butch Vig, Duke Erikson, and sound engineer Steve Marker, who specifically sought a female singer in the vein of Chrissie Hynde or Patty Smith, one who could sing in a lower register. "She was drafted into Garbage by three dudes, butch vig, the record producer, Duke Erickson, and another producer and sound engineer named Steve Marker."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Later Revival Artist & Ohio Home
xref.body: The Black Keys are noted as a later band in the Garage Rock revival. Their home city of Akron, Ohio, is also highlighted as the original home of Chrissie Hynde and The Pretenders, and a regional influence for Karen O. of the Ye-Eyes. "And just an hour away was Akron, the original home of Christy Hine and the pretenders, and the home of the Black Keys."

xref.title: Marriage to Chrissie Hynde
xref.body: Jim Kerr, the singer of Simple Minds, was married to Chrissie Hynde of The Pretenders at the time his band was being pressured to record "Don't You (Forget About Me)" for *The Breakfast Club* soundtrack. Hynde's personal appeal to the band was instrumental in convincing them to record the song, which became their biggest hit. "But the label kept up the pressure and Chrissy Holland at the pretenders, who was married to Singer Jim Carr at the time, asked everyone in the band to reconsider."

xref.title: Pop Song Appreciation
xref.body: Despite her strong punk background, Chrissie Hynde also recognized and valued the appeal and power of a well-crafted pop song, integrating this sensibility into The Pretenders' music. "But she also appreciated the power and the value of a good pop song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious Marriage Attempt
xref.body: Chrissie Hynde notably almost married Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols, an attempt to acquire the British equivalent of a green card to remain in the UK. This anecdote further illustrates her deep connections within the early punk scene. "And then there was also the time that she nearly married Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols just so she could stay in the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious Marriage Plot
xref.body: Chrissie Hynde almost entered into a marriage of convenience with Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols as a means to remain in the UK and continue her musical work. "And she almost entered into a marriage of convenience with Sid Vicious of the Sex pistols, just so she could stay in the UK and work."

xref.title: Simple Minds' "Don't You (Forget About Me)" Advocacy
xref.body: Chrissie Hynde, lead singer of The Pretenders and then married to Simple Minds singer Jim Kerr, played a crucial role in convincing Simple Minds to record "Don't You (Forget About Me)." Despite the band's reluctance to record an outsider's song, Hynde's intervention contributed to them reconsidering and ultimately recording what would become their biggest hit. "But the label kept up the pressure and Chrissy Holland at the pretenders, who was married to Singer Jim Carr at the time, asked everyone in the band to reconsider."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sire Records Endorsement
xref.body: Seymour Stein, head of Sire Records, was drawn to The Pretenders, appreciating their edgy, punky sound, songwriting talent, and the image of a strong American woman (Chrissie Hynde) fronting a band that was 75% English, which he saw as the epitome of New Wave. "To him, it didn't get any more new wave than that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unplayed Gigs
xref.body: This band is described as "the most famous British punk band to never play a gig." Despite many people, including Chrissie Hynde, flowing through its lineup, "nothing really happened with the London SS," which merely possessed "promise and potential." "The Clash evolved out of the most famous British punk band to never play a gig. They were called the London SS."
